dedupe_keys.name: white cart water flood prevention scheme catchment approach to flash floods in glasgow uk

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the White Cart Water flood prevention scheme in the south side of Glasgow, Scotland, where the river can rise six metres after twelve hours of rain and caused more than 20 significant floods in a century. Studies from 1984 led to a scheme, developed from 2002, promoted by Glasgow City Council in 2004 and approved by the Scottish Government in 2006, that combines three upstream flood storage areas in the rural catchment with urban flood defences, designed for the 1 in 200 year event, which corresponds to about 1 in 100 years by the 2050s under the climate projections used. Construction ran from 2008 to 2011 in two contracts worth 53 million pounds (63 million euro), with an 80% Scottish Government grant, and a further 3 km of defence wall was planned under the Clyde and Loch Lomond flood risk management plan. The page is free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal, drawing on Covenant of Mayors good practice. Caveats: benefits are stated as reduced predicted risk, not observed performance, and the scheme is one catchment. It illustrates catchment-scale storage combined with urban defences for pluvial and fluvial flooding; a related record is the EPA National Stormwater Calculator.
name: White Cart Water flood prevention scheme, catchment approach to flash floods in Glasgow (UK)
outcomes: Three upstream storage areas and urban defences built 2008 to 2011 for 53 million pounds protect suburban Glasgow to a 1 in 200 year standard, about 1 in 100 years by the 2050s.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study on Glasgow City Council
resources_used: climate change allowance on the 1 in 200 year design event
